extracted.intended_audience: astronomers and mathematical practitioners determining comet positions and orbits (historical/technical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Geometric and observational procedures to compute a comet's parabolic trajectory and associated physical inferences from telescopic observations; includes divided-difference interpolation, specific geometric constructions, observational protocols, and evidential criteria for interpreting comet tails and nucleus properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divided-differences interpolation for unequally spaced abscissas
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure for unequally spaced abscissas: 'L, &c. inæqualia sint intervalla HI, IK, &c. collige perpendiculorum AH, BI, CK, &c. differentias primas per intervalla perpendiculorum divisas b, 2b, 3b, 4b, 5b; secundas per intervalla bina divisas c, 2c, 3c, 4c, &c. tertias per intervalla terna divisas d, 2d, 3d, &c. quartas per intervalla quaterna divisas e, 2e, &c. & sic deinceps; id est ita ut sit b = {AH - BI} ÷ HI, 2b = {BI - CK} ÷ IK, 3b = {CK - DL} ÷ KL &c. dein c = {b - 2b} ÷ HK, ... Postea d = {c - 2c} ÷ HL, ... Inventis differentiis, dic AH = a, - HS = p, p in - IS = q, ... & erit ordinatim applicata RS = a + bp + cq + dr + es + ft, &c.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the explicit divided-difference scheme (Newton-style) for approximating the ordinate of a curve at an intermediate abscissa when abscissas are unequal. Follow the stepwise computation of first, second, third... differences divided by the appropriate interval lengths, then form the polynomial-like sum a + bp + cq + dr + ..., which gives RS (the desired ordinate). The text uses this to approximate points on a regular curve drawn through observed points and to derive areas approximately (Coroll.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of observations required depends on size of observed differences
rubrics_metrics.description: ''Si longitudinum observatarum parvæ sint differentiæ, puta graduum tantum 4 vel 5; suffecerint observationes tres vel quatuor ad inveniendam longitudinem & latitudinem novam. Sin majores sint differentiæ, puta graduum 10 vel 20, debebunt observationes quinque adhiberi.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule-of-thumb for sufficiency of data for interpolation/curve-fitting: when observed changes between measures are small, 3–4 observations suffice to interpolate a new longitude/latitude; when changes are large, more (≈5) observations are necessary. Use this to decide whether to apply the simpler three-point constructions or to gather additional observations and use the higher-order divided-difference interpolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct through a given point a line whose parts have a given ratio (Lemma VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma statement: '_Per datum punctum P ducere rectam lineam BC, cujus partes PB, PC, rectis duabus positione datis AB, AC abscissæ, datam habeant rationem ad invicem._' Construction: from P draw any PD to AB, extend to E so that PE:PD equals the given ratio; take AD parallel to EC; then in triangle CPB, PC:PB = PE:PD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this geometric construction when one must draw a line through a point so that its segments cut off on two given rays are in a prescribed ratio. The lemma provides a straightforward construction and a short proof (Q.E.F.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic chord segment approximately proportional to time (Lemma VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma statement: in parabola ABC with chord AC bisected in I, construct point E on AC via the given geometric construction (I[mu], [mu]O half of I[mu], draw OS, extend to [xi] so S[xi] = 2SO, draw [xi]B cutting AC at E) and then: 'dico quod punctum E abscindet de chorda AC segmentum AE tempori proportionale quamproximè.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an explicit geometric rule to find on chord AC a segment AE that is approximately proportional to the time taken by the comet to traverse the corresponding arc. The lemma's proof reduces the problem to comparing areas (AEY to ACY) and uses simple ratios derived from the constructed points; apply when approximating times from parabolic arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate chord length via velocity at an altitude (Lemmas X and Corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma X and its corollary state that if the comet were to proceed with the velocity it has at altitude S[mu] + 2/3 I[mu], then in the same time it would describe (approximately) the chord AC: 'Cometa igitur ea cum velocitate, quam habet in altitudine S[mu] + 2/3I[mu], eodem tempore describeret chordam AC quamproximè.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the velocity at a suitably chosen altitude (Sμ + 2/3 Iμ) as an estimator to convert arc-lengths into chord lengths (or vice versa). This provides a practical approximation linking instantaneous velocities at altitudes to finite chord lengths, used in geometric orbit constructions and time-to-distance conversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of orbital arc and vertical descent under specified impulsive force (Lemma XI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma XI: 'Si Cometa motu omni privatus de altitudine SN seu S[mu] + 1/3I[mu] demitteretur, ut caderet in Solem, & ea semper vi uniformiter continuata urgeretur in Solem qua urgetur sub initio; idem tempore in orbe suo describat arcum AC, descensu suo describeret spatium longitudini I[mu] æquale.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma gives a mechanical analogy: if the comet were suddenly deprived of its tangential motion and fell toward the Sun under a continuously applied force equal to its initial solar-directed attraction, then the distance fallen would equal a certain orbital chord length. Use this as a means to relate orbital motion to equivalent straight-line motions in deducing chord lengths or time intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric algorithm to determine a comet's parabolic trajectory from three observations (Prop. XLI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition statement and construction begin: 'Cometæ in Parabola moventis Trajectoriam ex datis tribus observationibus determinare.' Steps include selecting three observations (nearly equal time intervals), drawing circumferences through the three observed directions A,B,C and bisecting AC in i, constructing chord AC and bisector I, erecting perpendiculars AM, CN, IO, constructing rectangle iI[lambda][mu], taking I[sigma] = 3 I[lambda], forming σξ = 3 S[σ] + 3 i[λ], removing letters and drawing occult BE adjusted by distance ratio S[mu]+1/3 i[lambda], repeating AC construction so its parts AE and EC are in ratio of the observation intervals V:W, etc.; further constructions give MP, MN, NP and finally the orbit plane intersections X,Z and the two possible comet positions in its own plane, from which the parabola with focus S is drawn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the detailed geometric construction as given to compute the parabola passing through the three observational directions. Important practical notes: choose the three observations with approximately equal time spacing; compute intermediate constructed points (E, i, rectangle corners, etc.) exactly per directions; the proposition includes an explicit worked example. The construction yields two possible positions in the comet's orbital plane; use tangents and arcs to determine the correct trajectory (see Prop. XIX Lib. I referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select initial proximate points and iterate refinement for B, b, β
rubrics_metrics.description: From the construction: 'Cæterum puncta B, b, [beta] non quælibet, sed vero proxima eligere convenit.' The text prescribes an initial choice of B via an occult line SEB whose part EB equals length Vt, then repeats the construction deleting and redrawing AC and refining points b and β by composed ratios until Bb is sufficiently small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When implementing the three-observation construction choose initial approximate positions for B close to the true ecliptic projection of the comet. Use the provided rule (construct SEB so EB = Vt as a first guess), compute MP and MN etc., then adjust B to b (and to β if needed) via the composite ratio laws given. Usually two iterations suffice; stop when the displacement Bb is negligibly small and the constructed circumferences meet in the expected points X and Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational protocol to reduce systematic error (Flamsteed's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical observing method used by Flamsteed: 'postquam bis observasset distantiam Cometæ à Stella aliqua fixa, deinde etiam distantiam bis ab alia stella fixa, rediret ad stellam priorem & distantiam Cometæ ab eadem iterum observaret, idque bis, ac deinde ex distantiæ illius incremento vel decremento tempori proportionali colligeret distantiam tempore intermedio.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure distances to one fixed star twice, then twice to another star, then again twice to the first star (i.e., repeat measurements in alternation). From the increment/decrement of these distances proportional to time, interpolate the comet's separation at intermediate times. This reduces observational bias and permits more reliable interpolations for orbit computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental technique and expected observational errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrumentation: 'Hæ observationes Telescopio septupedali, & Micrometro filisque in foco Telescopii locatis paractæ sunt.' Error claim: 'Longitudinum tamen & Latitudinum errores ... dimidium minuti unius primi vix superant, præterquam in observatione ultimâ Mart. 9.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a long telescope with a micrometer wire or filaments at the focal plane to measure separations precisely. Expect typical errors of observed longitudes/latitudes to be under about 0.5' of arc under careful practice; note that some observations (e.g., when reference-star positions were determined less accurately) may have larger errors and should be downweighted or treated cautiously in orbit solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by comparing computed and observed positions over time
rubrics_metrics.description: After computing the orbit ('Orbem jam descriptum...'), compute comet positions at observation times and compare to measured longitudes and latitudes. The author tabulates computed vs observed values and their differences, asserting that congruence within observational and graphical-computation errors confirms the orbit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the computed orbital elements to predict positions at observation epochs and tabulate differences in longitude and latitude. If discrepancies are within the estimated combined observational and computational errors, the proposed orbit is accepted; check agreement across months (including earlier observations if available) for further confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidential criteria that comet tails are material vapors (rejecting purely optical/refraction theories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument summary: tails become largest and brightest immediately after passage near the Sun; tails are seen even when nucleus light is weak; tails curve and deviate consistent with nucleus motion; tails do not display refraction-based colour patterns; telescopes dramatically increase stellar brightness but do not reveal tails on stars or planets; repeated similar comet observations in different apparitions show different tail deviations incompatible with a fixed atmospheric refraction cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To conclude that comet tails are composed of real matter (vapor/dust) and not merely optical or atmospheric refraction effects, assemble these observational facts: (1) maximal tails after perihelion (heating effect), (2) tails present when nucleus faint (material necessary to reflect light), (3) tails' systematic deviations and curvature correlate with comet motion and viewing geometry, (4) absence of similar tails in telescopic views of stars/planets argues against a universal refractive medium. Use these points as mutually reinforcing evidence to reject optical/refraction explanations and favor material emission from the nucleus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference that cometary nuclei are solid/compact from heating arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument: if comets were mere vapors/exhalations they would be immediately dissipated near the Sun due to intense solar heating; scaling heat-loss arguments (heated iron sphere thought-experiment) indicate a large body can retain heat for very long times, so comets must be solid, compact, and durable like planetary bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use energy-density and heat-loss scaling to evaluate whether a comet could be vaporous and survive perihelion. The text's heuristic (comparing solar heating at comet perihelion to terrestrial heating, and comparing to heat retention of large heated masses) supports solidity; treat this as a physical-interpretation criterion when evaluating hypotheses about comet constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail rarity and low density inferred from star transmission and atmospheric-column arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation and calculation: many stars are visible through comet tails without significant dimming, implying extreme tenuity. The author compares the mass/column of terrestrial air to hypothetical cometary atmospheres (using ratios of column weights and gravitational/pressure scaling) to argue that cometary comas and tails, while enormously extended, are of extremely low density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transmission of starlight through tails and quantitative comparisons of columnar densities to estimate that cometary atmospheres and tails are extremely rarefied. This supports treating tails as tenuous vapour/dust clouds rather than dense gaseous envelopes; include the crude columnar computations as order-of-magnitude checks on physical models.
